title: Why functions are useful, and how to use them effectively
recap: Functions reduce a larger program into named operations that can be understood, reused, and checked independently. A well-defined interface lets callers rely on an operation without needing to follow every implementation detail.

Prefer functions with one clear responsibility and explicit inputs and outputs. Calculation and presentation are different jobs: return computed data first, then let separate reporting code decide how to display it.
objectives: Separate a workflow into small functions with distinct responsibilities.
Keep reusable calculations independent of console presentation.
Connect function outputs to later function inputs.
Use main() to coordinate operations rather than implement every detail.
warnings: Keeping all behavior in main() makes growing programs harder to navigate and test.
Copying a calculation creates multiple places that can drift or contain different mistakes.
A function that calculates and prints has two responsibilities and is less reusable.
Long or unfocused functions should be divided along meaningful task boundaries.
challenge: Implement calculateRoofArea(int length, int width), calculateRunoffUnits(int area, int rainfallUnits), and printDrainageReport(int area, int runoffUnits). Use length 12, width 8, and rainfall factor 3 in main(). Calculate the area, use that result to calculate runoff, and call the reporting function once. The two calculation functions must only return computed values; all console output belongs in printDrainageReport().
hints: First, implement calculateRoofArea by returning the product of its two parameters without printing anything.

Pseudocode: FUNCTION calculateRoofArea(length, width): RETURN length * width. FUNCTION calculateRunoffUnits(area, rainfallUnits): RETURN area * rainfallUnits. FUNCTION printDrainageReport(area, runoffUnits): OUTPUT the roof-area label, area, and unit text; OUTPUT the runoff-load label, runoffUnits, and unit text. MAIN: area = calculateRoofArea(12, 8); runoffUnits = calculateRunoffUnits(area, 3); call printDrainageReport(area, runoffUnits); return success.

Near-C++ structure: int calculateRoofArea(int length, int width) { return /* product of the dimensions */; } int calculateRunoffUnits(int area, int rainfallUnits) { return /* area scaled by rainfallUnits */; } void printDrainageReport(int area, int runoffUnits) { std::cout << /* area report pieces */; std::cout << /* runoff report pieces */; } int main() { int area{/* required area call */}; int runoffUnits{/* required runoff call */}; /* call the report function, then return success */ }
